parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.

The world's first cities

The creation of Mesopotamian cities

The inhabitants of Mesopotamia, which now lies within Iraq and parts of eastern Syria and southeastern Turkey, lived for thousands of years on individual farms or in small, isolated communities, working relentlessly just to meet their basic needs. But then, about 6,000 years ago, something remarkable happened. The people left the security of their family homes and villages and came together to create something far more complex and difficult: the world’s first city, Uruk.

Not much of Uruk remains today. Located about 250 kilometres south of Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, enough of the city survives to show that this initial experiment in urban living was extraordinarily successful. At its height, around 5,000 years ago, Uruk was home to more than 40,000 people. The outlines of the city walls indicate an enclosed area of about 600 hectares.

The archaeological record of Uruk reveals intensive building and rebuilding that continued for four or five centuries after the city was established. During this period, the people of Uruk built a dozen or so large public buildings. They would carefully level the previous structure and then build another on top, often experimenting with a different building material or an innovative technique. They seemed to be searching for ways in which architecture could express the new social structures that had come into being there.

Soon, Uruk was not the only Mesopotamian city. People throughout the flat plains of southern Mesopotamia were enjoying many of the benefits of city life. By about 4,500 years ago, 80 per cent of the Mesopotamian population lived in cities over 40 hectares in size, with populations of between 15,000 and 30,000. The emergence of these thriving communities, made up largely of people who were not related by blood, was unprecedented in human history. Why did these extraordinary developments occur?

Reasons for the creation of cities in Mesopotamia

Smaller communities in Mesopotamia sometimes decided to come together to defend themselves more effectively from their enemies. But the underlying reason for the creation of cities lay in the harshness of this particular environment. The area was a place of extremes, where narrow fertile river valleys were bounded by thousands of kilometres of desert and unproductive wetlands.

As the low level of rainfall in the region was insufficient to sustain more than very limited agriculture, it was only through sophisticated irrigation that isolated areas of land could be kept fertile. The Tigris and Euphrates rivers provided water for irrigation and also formed the basis of a communication network that led to the spread of the latest farming ideas.

In such a region, the only way for people to prosper was to form groups that could work together. The threat of famine, which could be caused by a prolonged drought or a sudden change in the course of a river, forced people to look beyond their families and work with their neighbours to create an elaborate system of dams, channels and canals to manage water. These projects required specific skills and labour from beyond the farmer’s own family. This reliance on people outside the family more firmly established the patterns of dependence that are at the heart of civilization.

Changes in the organisation of farming

The intensive farming that developed in Mesopotamia was more efficient and productive and therefore generated a surplus of food, allowing crops from good harvests to be stored as a safeguard against poorer harvests in future years. It also allowed more land to be used for the production of a wider range of crops. This created a need for traders and skilled craftsmen; in short, it marked the beginning of industry and consumerism.

Specialisation emerged within the population, with increasing numbers of soldiers, builders, musicians, doctors and fortune-tellers, all supported directly or indirectly by agriculture. At the same time, this growing specialisation increased the control that powerful institutions, gradually emerging in the early cities, had over the urban population. Although large numbers of people were freed from the struggle of subsistence farming, they were now totally dependent on the institutions that employed them for their daily sustenance.

The role of the temples

The earliest and most powerful of these institutions was centred on the temple. Increasing numbers of temple structures were erected as massive pyramids with enormous storerooms for produce from the farming estates. Over time, the temples acquired these farms and appointed a large number of staff to administer them and manage the storage of produce.

The temples’ greatest advantage was that each citizen was expected to devote some time to working for them. This allowed the temples to store huge amounts of agricultural produce, which could then be used to buy more land. In addition, the revenue they generated allowed the temples to serve as primitive banks by making loans to people during difficult economic times.

The emergence of writing

We know a surprising amount about this period thanks to the development of an important new technology: writing. In Mesopotamia, basic records were inscribed on wet clay rather than on the fragile papyrus used in ancient Egypt and Greece. These first writings were largely lists of people and things used for simple bookkeeping. But within several hundred years, writing systems had become more advanced and capable of recording concepts as well as lists. The clay tablets used for writing were durable, and fires that destroyed the archives where they were stored often simply baked the tablets, preserving them for future generations.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

The Cultures of Chimpanzees

A

The similarities between chimpanzees and humans have been studied for years, and research conducted over a decade has shown that these resemblances run much deeper than was previously thought. For instance, the nut-cracking behaviour observed in the Taï Forest is far from simple; rather, it is a distinctive adaptation found only in that particular part of Africa and a trait that biologists regard as an expression of chimpanzee culture. Scientists frequently use the term ‘culture’ to describe simple animal behaviours—such as regional dialects among different songbird populations—but the rich and varied cultural traditions found among chimpanzees are second only to human traditions in complexity.

B

Over a two-year period, an unprecedented scientific collaboration involving every major research group studying chimpanzees documented numerous distinct cultural patterns across Africa, ranging from tool use to forms of communication and social customs. This emerging picture of chimpanzees not only affects how we think of these animals but also alters our conception of our own uniqueness and hints at the ancient foundations of our extraordinary capacity for culture.

C

Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes have coexisted for hundreds of millennia and share more than 98 per cent of their genetic material, yet until systematic field studies began in the 1960s, very little was known about chimpanzee behaviour in the wild. This changed when Toshisada Nishida of Kyoto University in Japan and Jane Goodall began studying wild chimpanzees at two field sites in Tanzania. Goodall’s research station at Gombe—the first of its kind—is more famous, while Nishida’s site at Mahale is the second-oldest chimpanzee research site in the world.

D

In these initial studies, as the chimpanzees became accustomed to close observation, remarkable findings began to emerge. Researchers witnessed a range of unexpected behaviours, including fashioning and using tools, hunting, meat-eating, food sharing and lethal fights between members of neighbouring communities. In the years that followed, other primatologists established research sites elsewhere, and despite the financial, political and logistical problems that can beset fieldwork in Africa, several of these sites developed into long-term projects. As a result, these studies have produced a detailed and comprehensive scientific record of chimpanzees’ lives, not just for one but for several communities spread across Africa.

E

As early as 1973, Goodall recorded 13 forms of tool use as well as eight social activities. These appeared to differ between the Gombe chimpanzees and populations elsewhere. She suggested that some of these variations had what she termed a cultural origin. But what exactly did Goodall mean by “culture”? According to the Oxford Encyclopedic English Dictionary, culture is defined as “the customs … and achievements of a particular time or people.” The diversity of human cultures extends from technological variations to marriage rituals, from culinary habits to myths and legends. Animals do not have myths and legends. But they do have the capacity to pass on behavioural traits from generation to generation, not through genetic inheritance but through learning. For biologists, this is the fundamental criterion for a cultural trait: it must be something that can be learned by observing skills already practised by others and thus passed on to future generations.

F

What, then, are the implications for chimpanzees themselves? Chimpanzee populations are declining severely even as scientific understanding of these animals has become more complete. Their numbers have fallen dramatically over roughly a century and continue to decline as a result of illegal trapping, logging and the bushmeat trade. The bushmeat trade is particularly alarming: logging has led to roads being built into the forests, which are used to transport meat from wild animals—including chimpanzee meat—to consumers as far away as Europe. Such destruction threatens not only the animals themselves but also a diverse range of ape cultures.

G

However, the cultural richness of chimpanzees may itself contribute to their conservation. Some conservation efforts have altered the attitudes of some local people. A few organisations have begun to show videotapes illustrating the cognitive abilities of chimpanzees. One Zairian viewer exclaimed, “Ah, this ape is so like me, I can no longer eat him.”

H

The international team of chimpanzee experts conducted the most comprehensive survey of chimpanzees ever attempted. Scientists had been investigating chimpanzee culture for several decades, but many of their studies shared a crucial limitation. Most previous attempts to document cultural diversity among chimpanzees had relied solely on published reports of the behaviours recorded at each research site. This approach was likely to overlook considerable cultural variation for three reasons.

I

First, scientists typically did not publish extensive records of activities that were not observed at a particular site. Yet knowing which behaviours were and were not observed at each site was essential. Second, many reports described chimpanzee behaviours without indicating how common they were; without this information, researchers could not determine whether a particular action was an isolated occurrence or a routine event that should be considered part of the animals’ culture. Finally, researchers’ descriptions of potentially significant chimpanzee behaviours frequently lacked sufficient detail, making it difficult for scientists working at other sites to determine whether those behaviours were present or absent.

J

To address these problems, the researchers adopted a new approach. Field researchers at each site were asked to provide a list of all behaviours they suspected were local traditions. Using this information, the researchers compiled a comprehensive list of 65 candidate cultural behaviours.

K

The resulting list was then distributed to the team leaders at each site. In consultation with their colleagues, the team leaders classified each behaviour according to its occurrence or absence in the chimpanzee community being studied. The key categories were customary, habitual, present, absent and unknown. A behaviour was classified as customary if it was observed in most or all able-bodied members of at least one age or sex class, such as all adult males; habitual if it was less common than customary but occurred repeatedly in several individuals; present if it had been observed at the site but was not habitual; and absent if it had never been observed at the site.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

The Cultures of Chimpanzees

A

The similarities between chimpanzees and humans have been studied for years, and research conducted over a decade has shown that these resemblances run much deeper than was previously thought. For instance, the nut-cracking behaviour observed in the Taï Forest is far from simple; rather, it is a distinctive adaptation found only in that particular part of Africa and a trait that biologists regard as an expression of chimpanzee culture. Scientists frequently use the term ‘culture’ to describe simple animal behaviours—such as regional dialects among different songbird populations—but the rich and varied cultural traditions found among chimpanzees are second only to human traditions in complexity.

B

Over a two-year period, an unprecedented scientific collaboration involving every major research group studying chimpanzees documented numerous distinct cultural patterns across Africa, ranging from tool use to forms of communication and social customs. This emerging picture of chimpanzees not only affects how we think of these animals but also alters our conception of our own uniqueness and hints at the ancient foundations of our extraordinary capacity for culture.

C

Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes have coexisted for hundreds of millennia and share more than 98 per cent of their genetic material, yet until systematic field studies began in the 1960s, very little was known about chimpanzee behaviour in the wild. This changed when Toshisada Nishida of Kyoto University in Japan and Jane Goodall began studying wild chimpanzees at two field sites in Tanzania. Goodall’s research station at Gombe—the first of its kind—is more famous, while Nishida’s site at Mahale is the second-oldest chimpanzee research site in the world.

D

In these initial studies, as the chimpanzees became accustomed to close observation, remarkable findings began to emerge. Researchers witnessed a range of unexpected behaviours, including fashioning and using tools, hunting, meat-eating, food sharing and lethal fights between members of neighbouring communities. In the years that followed, other primatologists established research sites elsewhere, and despite the financial, political and logistical problems that can beset fieldwork in Africa, several of these sites developed into long-term projects. As a result, these studies have produced a detailed and comprehensive scientific record of chimpanzees’ lives, not just for one but for several communities spread across Africa.

E

As early as 1973, Goodall recorded 13 forms of tool use as well as eight social activities. These appeared to differ between the Gombe chimpanzees and populations elsewhere. She suggested that some of these variations had what she termed a cultural origin. But what exactly did Goodall mean by “culture”? According to the Oxford Encyclopedic English Dictionary, culture is defined as “the customs … and achievements of a particular time or people.” The diversity of human cultures extends from technological variations to marriage rituals, from culinary habits to myths and legends. Animals do not have myths and legends. But they do have the capacity to pass on behavioural traits from generation to generation, not through genetic inheritance but through learning. For biologists, this is the fundamental criterion for a cultural trait: it must be something that can be learned by observing skills already practised by others and thus passed on to future generations.

F

What, then, are the implications for chimpanzees themselves? Chimpanzee populations are declining severely even as scientific understanding of these animals has become more complete. Their numbers have fallen dramatically over roughly a century and continue to decline as a result of illegal trapping, logging and the bushmeat trade. The bushmeat trade is particularly alarming: logging has led to roads being built into the forests, which are used to transport meat from wild animals—including chimpanzee meat—to consumers as far away as Europe. Such destruction threatens not only the animals themselves but also a diverse range of ape cultures.

G

However, the cultural richness of chimpanzees may itself contribute to their conservation. Some conservation efforts have altered the attitudes of some local people. A few organisations have begun to show videotapes illustrating the cognitive abilities of chimpanzees. One Zairian viewer exclaimed, “Ah, this ape is so like me, I can no longer eat him.”

H

The international team of chimpanzee experts conducted the most comprehensive survey of chimpanzees ever attempted. Scientists had been investigating chimpanzee culture for several decades, but many of their studies shared a crucial limitation. Most previous attempts to document cultural diversity among chimpanzees had relied solely on published reports of the behaviours recorded at each research site. This approach was likely to overlook considerable cultural variation for three reasons.

I

First, scientists typically did not publish extensive records of activities that were not observed at a particular site. Yet knowing which behaviours were and were not observed at each site was essential. Second, many reports described chimpanzee behaviours without indicating how common they were; without this information, researchers could not determine whether a particular action was an isolated occurrence or a routine event that should be considered part of the animals’ culture. Finally, researchers’ descriptions of potentially significant chimpanzee behaviours frequently lacked sufficient detail, making it difficult for scientists working at other sites to determine whether those behaviours were present or absent.

J

To address these problems, the researchers adopted a new approach. Field researchers at each site were asked to provide a list of all behaviours they suspected were local traditions. Using this information, the researchers compiled a comprehensive list of 65 candidate cultural behaviours.

K

The resulting list was then distributed to the team leaders at each site. In consultation with their colleagues, the team leaders classified each behaviour according to its occurrence or absence in the chimpanzee community being studied. The key categories were customary, habitual, present, absent and unknown. A behaviour was classified as customary if it was observed in most or all able-bodied members of at least one age or sex class, such as all adult males; habitual if it was less common than customary but occurred repeatedly in several individuals; present if it had been observed at the site but was not habitual; and absent if it had never been observed at the site.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Personality and appearance

When Charles Darwin applied to serve as a gentleman companion to Robert Fitzroy, the Beagle’s captain, who was seeking an “energetic young man”, he was nearly rejected because of a supposed shortcoming that was as plain as the nose on his face. Fitzroy believed in physiognomy—the idea that a person’s character can be inferred from their appearance. As Darwin’s daughter Henrietta later recalled, Fitzroy had “made up his mind that no man with such a nose could have energy”. This judgment was far from accurate. Fortunately, the rest of Darwin’s visage compensated for his sluggardly proboscis: “His brow saved him.”

The idea that a person’s character can be glimpsed in their face dates back to the ancient Greeks. It was most notably popularised in the late 18th century by the Swiss poet Johann Lavater, whose ideas became a talking point in intellectual circles. By Darwin’s time, such ideas were largely accepted without question. It was only after physiognomy became associated with phrenology, which fell into disrepute in the late 19th century, that physiognomy was dismissed as pseudoscience.

First impressions are highly influential, despite the well-worn admonition not to judge a book by its cover. Within a tenth of a second of seeing an unfamiliar face, we form a judgment about the person’s character—caring, trustworthy, aggressive, extroverted, competent, and so on. Once formed, that snap judgment is surprisingly difficult to change. People also act on these snap judgments. Politicians with competent-looking faces are more likely to be elected, and CEOs who look dominant are more likely to head profitable companies. There is also a well-established “attractiveness halo”. People seen as good-looking not only get the most valentines but are also judged to be more outgoing, socially competent, powerful, intelligent, and healthy.

In 1966, psychologists at the University of Michigan asked 84 undergraduates who had never met one another before to rate one another on five personality traits solely on the basis of appearance, while they sat for 15 minutes in silence. For three traits—extroversion, conscientiousness, and openness—their rapid judgments corresponded with actual personality scores significantly more often than would be expected by chance. In later research, Anthony Little of the University of Stirling and David Perrett of the University of St Andrews, both in the UK, re-examined the link between appearance and personality. They pointed out that the Michigan research was not tightly controlled for confounding factors. But when Little and Perrett re-ran the experiment using mugshots rather than live subjects, they also found a link between facial appearance and personality—though only for extroversion and conscientiousness. They reported that the correlation appeared only at the extremes of personality.

Justin Carre and Cheryl McCormick of Brock University in Ontario, Canada, studied 90 ice hockey players. They found that a higher ratio of cheekbone-to-cheekbone distance to the distance between the brow and upper lip was significantly associated with the number of penalty minutes players received for violent acts, including slashing, elbowing, checking from behind and fighting. Findings such as these suggest that there may be a kernel of truth in facial judgments. However, this is not the only explanation for our readiness to make them. Leslie Zebrowitz, a psychologist at Brandeis University in Waltham, Massachusetts, says that in many cases snap judgments are not accurate. Such judgments, she says, are often an “overgeneralisation” of a more fundamental response. A classic example of overgeneralisation is predators’ response to eye spots, the conspicuous circular markings found on some moths, butterflies and fish. These markings deter predators because they mimic the eyes of creatures that may be perceived as threatening.

Another researcher who leans towards overgeneralisation is Alexander Todorov. Together with Princeton colleague Nikolaas Oosterhof, he put forward a theory to explain snap judgments of faces in terms of how threatening they appear. Todorov and Oosterhof asked people for their immediate reactions to pictures of emotionally neutral faces, analysed the responses, and reduced them to two underlying factors: how trustworthy and how dominant each face appeared. They concluded that personality judgments based on faces are an overgeneralisation of an evolved ability to read emotions from facial expressions and, from them, infer a person’s intention and ability to cause harm. Todorov, however, stresses that overgeneralisation does not rule out the idea that there is sometimes a kernel of truth in such personality assessments.

If there is a kernel of truth, then where does it come from? Perrett suspects that the link arises when our prejudices about faces turn into self-fulfilling prophecies—an idea investigated by other researchers in 1977. Our expectations can influence other people’s behaviour in ways that eventually confirm those expectations: if someone is consistently treated as untrustworthy, they may eventually behave that way. Sometimes, however, the effect works in the opposite direction, particularly for people who look cute. The Nobel Prize-winning ethologist Konrad Lorenz once suggested that baby-faced features evoke a nurturing response. Related work by Zebrowitz found that the sight of baby-faced boys and men stimulates the amygdala, an emotional centre of the brain. However, there is a twist. Baby-faced men are, on average, better educated and more assertive, and tend to win more military medals than their mature-looking counterparts. They are also more likely to be criminals; Al Capone is one example. Similarly, Zebrowitz found baby-faced boys to be quarrelsome and hostile, and more likely to be high academic achievers. She calls this the “self-defeating prophecy effect”: a man with a baby face strives to defy expectations and ends up overcompensating.

There is another theory that recalls the old parental warning not to pull faces because they might freeze that way. According to this theory, our personality moulds the way our faces look. Support for this theory comes from an earlier study which found that older people described as angry tended to look cross even when asked to adopt a neutral expression. A lifetime of scowling, grumpiness and grimaces seemed to have left its mark.
